A geometry in which Euclid's parallel postulate does not hold, first published by Nikolai Lobachevsky in Kazan in 1829. It is now called hyperbolic geometry.

For two thousand years mathematicians had tried to prove Euclid's fifth postulate: that through a point beside a line, exactly one parallel line can be drawn. Lobachevsky, a professor and later rector of Kazan University, took another path. He assumed that many such lines exist and worked out the results. He found no contradiction, only a strange but consistent world where the angles of a triangle add up to less than 180 degrees.

He published in a little read Kazan journal and was mostly ignored or mocked. The Hungarian János Bolyai reached the same ideas on his own in 1832, and Gauss had thought along these lines but kept quiet.

Later work by Bernhard Riemann and others showed that geometry need not be Euclidean. That freed mathematics to study many kinds of space, and it prepared the ground for Einstein's curved spacetime.
sum: A geometry in which Euclid's parallel postulate does not hold, first published by Nikolai Lobachevsky in Kazan in 1829. It is now called hyperbolic geometry.
